questions.prompt: In React Native's new architecture, what replaces the old asynchronous JSON-message bridge between JavaScript and native code?

options.label: WebSockets between the JS and native processes
JSI (JavaScript Interface) — a C++ layer that allows synchronous, typed JS-to-native calls
gRPC over Unix domain sockets
A shared SQLite database used as a message queue

questions.explanation: JSI is the C++ abstraction that replaces the bridge. JS holds direct references to native C++ objects and calls them synchronously, in the same thread, with no JSON serialization. Fabric (renderer) and TurboModules (native APIs) both build on top of JSI.

questions.prompt: What is the default JavaScript engine in modern React Native?

options.label: V8
JavaScriptCore (JSC)
Hermes
SpiderMonkey

questions.explanation: Hermes is the default since RN 0.70. Built by Meta specifically for mobile — precompiled bytecode shipped in the bundle (fast startup), low memory floor, small binary contribution. JSC is still selectable but rare in 2026.

questions.prompt: What is the default workflow for starting a new React Native app in 2026?

options.label: npx react-native init (bare workflow, native folders checked into the repo)
Expo (managed workflow) with EAS Build / Submit / Update
Cordova with the React plugin
Ignite CLI for the Infinite Red template

questions.explanation: `npx create-expo-app` plus EAS is the default in 2026. Managed workflow means no `ios/`/`android/` folders in your repo — they're regenerated from `app.json` and your installed Expo modules. Bare workflow is the escape hatch for specific vendor SDKs.

questions.prompt: What can you ship to existing installs via EAS Update (over-the-air, OTA) without going through app store review?

options.label: Any change — JS, native code, new permissions, new SDK versions
Only the JavaScript bundle and assets (images, fonts, JSON) — never native code changes
Only configuration changes in app.json
Only changes to existing screens, not new screens

questions.explanation: OTA ships only the JS bundle and assets. New native modules, new permissions, new URL schemes, new Info.plist entries, and Expo SDK upgrades all require a new native build and a fresh app store submission. Setting `runtimeVersion` enforces compatibility so users don't get a JS bundle that calls APIs their installed binary lacks.

questions.prompt: What's the canonical way to run an animation on the native UI thread in modern React Native, without going through the JS thread on every frame?

options.label: Use the built-in Animated API with useNativeDriver: true for every animation
Use Reanimated 3 worklets — JS functions that run on a separate UI-thread JS runtime via useSharedValue and useAnimatedStyle
Drop into native and write the animation in Swift / Kotlin directly
Use requestAnimationFrame inside useEffect on the main JS thread

questions.explanation: Reanimated 3 is the production answer. Worklets are JS functions the library serializes and runs on a second Hermes runtime on the UI thread. Gesture handler events and animation updates never touch the main JS thread, so 60-120 fps animations are stable under JS-side load. The old `useNativeDriver: true` only covers a subset of properties; worklets are the general solution.
